Who Are We?

Lumina Labs is a neo-research laboratory based in Southeast Asia. Our team specializes in web development and data science, and seeks to combine the 2 together in harmony.
summary: Lumina Labs' Analog Site Finder matches locations on the Moon and Mars with similar sites on Earth. Using 39 open datasets from NASA, USGS, and NOAA, our Python pipeline compares 11 environmental features across a standardized 0.25° grid. In under 0.1 seconds, it ranks 334,131 Earth land cells and identifies the ten best matches, explaining their suitability and research status. The tool independently rediscovered established analogs like Devon Island and the Danakil Depression while identifying new candidates in Saudi Arabia, the Canadian Arctic, and Antarctica. Its built-in Equipment Tester also evaluates NASA hardware, including VIPER and CADRE, against local conditions. By making Earth-based testing faster, cheaper, and more targeted, Analog Site Finder helps mission teams reduce risks before exploring other worlds.
details:
Analog Site Finder

Lumina Labs, A Southeast Asian Neo-Research Laboratory

What does it do and how does it work?

Analog Site Finder is a web tool for mission planners. You click a spot on the Moon or Mars, and it finds the 10 places on Earth that are most like it. You can then test real equipment against those places before anything leaves the planet where it works in three layers.

1. Data pipeline (Python)

The pipeline downloads 39 open datasets from NASA, USGS, NOAA and others, about 7 GB in total. It turns them into one global grid for each body at a resolution of 0.25° (cells of roughly 28 km). Each cell gets the same 11 features on every body:

  • Elevation, slope and roughness
  • Lowest and highest temperature, and the day–night temperature swing
  • Thermal inertia (how slowly the ground heats and cools) and aridity
  • Terrain class (regolith, basalt, rock, sand or ice), plus flags for ice and volcanic ground

Sources include:

  • Moon: LRO LOLA elevation and Diviner temperatures, LROC lava-tube pits, and LOLA's maps of permanently shadowed craters
  • Mars: MGS MOLA elevation, TES thermal inertia and albedo, and SWIM subsurface ice
  • Earth: ETOPO 2022 elevation, NASA POWER climate, and MODIS land cover

2. Scoring engine

For a chosen Moon or Mars spot, the engine scores all 334,131 Earth land cells. Each feature is standardized, and the differences are combined into a weighted distance, with penalties when terrain, ice or volcanic type differ. That distance becomes a 0–100 match score.

  • Results are spread out so the 10 matches are always at least ~165 km apart.
  • Each match says why it scored well (for example, "similar roughness, basalt terrain").
  • A match gets a Known analog badge if a curated research site (Devon Island, Danakil, Atacama…) lies within 150 km. Otherwise it is tagged New.

3. Website (React + Express)

The website has five tools:

  • Planetary Map: an Earth globe beside a Moon or Mars globe, where you save bases, landing sites and testing sites.
  • Analog Sites: searches with adjustable weights and toggles.
  • Equipment Tester: a four-step wizard. It checks real NASA hardware (VIPER, CADRE, a habitat module) against a site's measured conditions, or runs a 3D physics traversal that uses the target body's gravity, the site's slope and the terrain's friction.
  • Landing Sites and Bases: each keeps its saved sites and the history of simulations run against them.

An interactive walkthrough guides first-time users.

What benefits does it have?

  • New analogs, not just known ones. It scores the whole planet instead of a short hand-picked list. For Mare Tranquillitatis, its top match is a new basalt site in Saudi Arabia. It also proposes new Canadian Arctic sites for Jezero Crater and new Antarctic ice sites for Arcadia Planitia.
  • Checked against known sites. It found known analogs on its own: the Danakil Depression (ranks 3 and 6) and Lanzarote (rank 8) for Mare Tranquillitatis, and Haughton Crater on Devon Island for Jezero (rank 9) and Hellas (rank 6).
  • Explains itself. Every match lists the features that drove it, and a table compares the target with the match feature by feature.
  • Honest about weak matches. Scores are compared with the best match Earth could possibly offer, so a Moon site isn't marked "weak" just because the Moon is colder than anywhere on Earth. A warning appears only when a result truly falls short.
  • Fast and free. A search over all of Earth takes about 50–100 ms. The tool runs in a browser with no login or paid service, and all data sources are open and cited.

What is the intended impact?

Field-testing rovers, habitats and crews at Earth analogs costs far less than finding problems on the Moon or Mars. Today the list of analogs is small and mostly based on tradition. This tool gives planners, researchers and students a data-driven way to:

  • Find new, nearer or cheaper test sites, including in countries not usually considered
  • Tune a search to what matters for a given mission
  • See quickly whether a piece of equipment suits the conditions at a candidate base or landing site

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data pipeline: Python 3.11 with numpy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, pyhdf, geopandas, shapely and pyarrow, tested with pytest. It runs end to end on Kaggle in 66 minutes, and a clean rerun produced byte-identical grids.
  • Backend: Node 24, TypeScript, Express 5, Zod 4 and Prisma 7 with SQLite, tested with Vitest and Supertest.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4, React Router, react-globe.gl and three.js (3D globes and the rover simulation) and Axios, tested with Vitest and Testing Library.
  • Data: the 39 open datasets plus a USGS unified geologic map for each of the Moon and Mars. Every file is recorded with its URL, retrieval date and SHA-256 checksum. Free NASA Earthdata access is used.
  • Hardware: team laptops and a self-hosted Linux home server for staging. No special hardware.
  • Hosting: Used Vercel for hosting the demo.

How is the project creative?

  • One comparison across three worlds. The same 11 features are built for Earth, the Moon and Mars, so the three can be compared directly.
  • An Earth stand-in for thermal inertia. Earth has no global thermal-inertia map, so we use the day–night temperature swing as a stand-in, since ground that heats and cools slowly swings less.
  • Modelled Mars temperatures. There is no simple global map of Mars surface temperature to download, so we compute it for each cell from TES thermal inertia and albedo. The heat-balance model is checked against Viking and Curiosity measurements and never drops below the CO₂ frost point.
  • Scoring against the best possible match. Match quality is judged against the best analog Earth could possibly offer, not against a perfect copy.
  • Two matching scoring engines. The scoring is written in both Python and TypeScript and tested against a shared fixture, so the website returns exactly the scientists' numbers.
  • From finding a site to testing it. You go from "Where on Earth is like this crater?" to "Would VIPER make it up this slope?" in one place.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific honesty: no synthetic fallbacks. If a dataset failed to download, the pipeline stopped until we found the real one. Every judgement call is documented, for example counting Mars ice only poleward of 30°, after the simple rule flagged 25% of Mars, equator included.
    • At 0.25°, some small islands such as Lanzarote fall outside the land mask.
    • Cells that are mostly forest, farmland or city are excluded, which drops a few curated analogs (Rio Tinto, Pavilion Lake, Ries, Undara).
    • Earth's climate grid (0.5° × 0.625°) is coarser than the terrain grid.
  • Physics details: each body's own radius for slopes and distances, its own gravity in the simulation, and seafloor depths masked out of coastal cells.
  • Privacy: no accounts. Each browser gets an anonymous key, so visitors never see each other's saved sites.
  • Reproducibility: pinned data checksums, a one-click Kaggle notebook, and automated tests on every layer.
  • Performance and cost: precomputed grids (40 MB) and an optimized search. The whole thing runs on one small server.
  • Usability: a dark "mission control" design, color paired with icons for pass and fail, a mobile layout and a guided walkthrough.
